name: Expectations for this course

ans:
Communicate with lecturer/tutors for guidance
Attend lectures and tutorials
Start assignments early
Ask questions (alternative views welcome)
Be responsible

name: Science and the scientific method
q: How does the lecture define science and the scientific method?
ans:
Science: an approach to knowing that relies on observation, testing and falsification
Scientific method: a set of principles and procedures researchers use to develop questions, collect data and reach conclusions
Uses evidence (data) to answer research questions

name: Certainty in science
q: How certain is knowledge obtained through the scientific method?
ans:
Based on a degree of certainty
No claim in science is absolutely certain
Even more so in the psychological sciences

name: Scientific vs non-scientific questions
q: What distinguishes scientific questions from non-scientific questions?
ans:
Scientific: can be tested with the scientific method by collecting data (e.g. does sleep deprivation affect cognitive performance?)
Non-scientific: cannot be tested; usually philosophical, answered by argument
Non-scientific questions are subjective, shaped by opinions, personal beliefs and culture (e.g. does God exist?)

name: Steps of the scientific method
q: What are the basic steps of the scientific method?
ans:
Ask a question
Do background research
Construct hypotheses
Test with an experiment / collect data
Analyse data and draw conclusions (supported or not; loop back if not)
Report results

name: Research as a scientific conversation
q: What does it mean that scientific research is a 'conversation'?
ans:
An exchange of thoughts, information and arguments; each person adds something new and relevant
Happens when researchers publish work in scientific journals
Others read it, ask new questions and respond with their own studies
Disagreements are debated until a conclusion with the fewest errors or biases is reached

name: Participating in the scientific conversation
q: How can you participate in the scientific conversation?
ans:
Read research articles (preferably recent) to know what is being discussed
Critique weak arguments or questionable findings
Build/extend on findings, suggest alternative views, or conduct a new study
Listen to other researchers' responses to your studies; you are free to question anyone's claims

name: Scientific vs nonsensical conversation
q: What separates a scientific conversation from a nonsensical conversation (sleep example)?
ans:
Scientific: each reply adds something new AND relevant that builds on the claim (e.g. sleep amount differs for cognition vs mood; sleep quality matters)
Nonsensical: replies drift off-topic or rely on irrelevant anecdotes (lazy uncles, babies, koalas)

name: Variable
q: What is a variable, and what kinds of variables does Lecture 1 give as examples?
ans:
Something that is studied and can change in value
Traits: age, height, IQ, personality
Interventions/manipulations: caffeine, alcohol, smell
Outcomes: test marks, task performance

name: Causal vs non-causal relationship
q: What is the difference between a causal and a non-causal relationship?
clues: Related is not the same as caused
ans:
Causal: a change in one variable causes the change in another
Non-causal: the two variables are related, but one cannot be said to cause the other
Just because two variables are related does not mean one causes the other

name: Research question
q: What is a research question, and what two types can be formed?
ans:
Formed after identifying the variables of interest
Can ask about causal relationships (e.g. Can caffeine increase levels of attention?)
Can ask about non-causal relationships (e.g. Is there a relationship between self-esteem and academic grades?)

name: Hypothesis
q: What is a hypothesis and what makes a good one?
ans:
A prediction about the expected relationship between your variables
Good hypotheses have strong scientific backing, based on logical and relevant evidence
E.g. participants who drink coffee 3 hours before bed will have poorer sleep quality than those who don't

name: Obstacles to understanding scientific writing
q: How does the lecture suggest overcoming obstacles to understanding scientific writing?
ans:
Scientific writing is hard at first but you get used to it and become a more critical consumer
Start by reading the abstract
Most journals follow a particular format and structure; knowing each part helps you navigate

name: Types of professional writing
q: What types of professional writing will you produce at university versus at work?
ans:
University: essays, literature reviews, research proposals, critiques of journal articles, scientific/lab reports
Work: project reports, proposals/tenders, performance evaluations, coaching reports, professional correspondence

name: School vs university writing
q: How does writing in primary/secondary school differ from writing during and after university?
ans:
School: write as students; learn by accepting and memorising; not expected to question; excellence = rote memorisation
University: write as professionals-to-be; actively question, query and critique
Excellence = thinking critically, deriving own conclusions, communicating reasoning clearly
Knowing/remembering is not enough; you must support and justify what you say

name: Qualities of good scientific writing
q: What three qualities make good scientific writing?
ans:
Precise and succinct: get to the point; use precise terms for the phenomena studied
Purposeful: reports new data/findings and contributes to the scientific conversation
Persuasive: relies on good arguments to persuade, convince or defend ideas

name: Communicating in psychology
q: What is expected of you when communicating in psychology (e.g. the vaccines–autism dialogue)?
ans:
Convey understanding of human thought, emotion and behaviour
Integrate past research, compare and contrast findings, justify your position
Question what you read: is it sufficiently supported and credible?
Explain why YOU agree with a source, not just cite it

name: Argument (what it is and is not)
q: What is an argument, and what is an argument NOT?
ans:
A claim/assertion that something is true, supported by logical reasons for believing it
You tell the other person why you believe the assertion
Not a verbal fight; raising your voice or personal attacks means you've already lost

name: Good vs bad arguments
q: What makes a good argument better than a bad one in the depression-genetics and punishment examples?
ans:
Bad: relies on personal anecdotes/few cases (neighbour, friend, own father) and overclaims ('definitely')
Good: relies on research evidence from a larger sample (review: 70% of depressed Malaysians have a family member with depression)
Good arguments use cautious conclusions ('likely')
Personal experience (being hit yet paying taxes) does not justify a general claim

name: Joining the scientific conversation
q: Why do you need to understand what a scientific conversation is about before joining it?
ans:
To join, you need to know what is being discussed
Not all conversations have the same scientific quality
Understanding it helps you decide whether it is a conversation you want to/can join

name: Scholarly (scientific) literature
q: What can you expect from scholarly (scientific) literature?
ans:
Original empirical (data) or theoretical (theoretical arguments) work
Author is critical and reviews empirical/theoretical work
Author summarises, argues or defends arguments about that work
Produced and reviewed by experts/academics, with some verifiable measure of credibility

name: Journal articles vs academic books
q: How do journal articles differ from academic books/textbooks as sources of scientific literature?
clues: Compare scope, goals, review standard, recency, content
ans:
Scope: articles are targeted/focused; books cover broader topics
Goals: articles justify theories and test new ideas; books give an overview/synthesis of a domain
Review: articles have a high peer-review standard; books lower (not necessarily less credible)
Recency: articles more likely to have latest findings; books give a broader, historical view
Content: articles detail methodology; books briefly mention it and describe phenomena/theories

name: Empirical article
q: What is an empirical journal article?
ans:
Presents new, usually primary data, analysed to test hypotheses and answer a research question
Includes methods and analyses
Makes claims about the meaning of results
Most psychology empirical papers are quantitative with statistical analyses

name: Theoretical / conceptual article
q: What is a theoretical or conceptual journal article?
ans:
Author(s) present their own model/theory about a concept based on existing empirical findings
No new data is collected to generate the model/theory
Describes components within a concept, their characteristics and relationships

name: Review article
q: What is a review article and what two forms can it take?
ans:
Provides a summary of results/patterns/theories in a particular field
Highlights key themes in past research and proposes future directions
Either a systematic review or a meta-analysis

name: Conference proceedings
q: What are conference proceedings?
ans:
A collection of papers accepted at a conference
May be empirical, conceptual, theoretical or review papers
Also peer-reviewed before being accepted at the conference

name: Empirical vs theoretical article
q: What is the key difference between an empirical article and a theoretical/conceptual article?
ans:
Empirical: collects new (primary) data and analyses it to test hypotheses
Theoretical/conceptual: no new data; builds a model/theory from existing empirical findings

name: Peer review
q: What is peer review and why does it matter?
ans:
Review of an article by other experts (peers) in the field before it is allowed to be published
A form of quality control ensuring rigour and validity
Matters because findings can have implications for society at large

name: Peer review evaluation criteria
q: What aspects of a paper do reviewers judge during peer review?
ans:
Value and novelty of findings
Soundness of methods
Consistency of results
Strength of arguments
Language and grammar

name: Peer review process and outcomes
q: What are the steps and possible outcomes of the (simplified) peer-review process?
ans:
Submission, then 1st screening for basic criteria (fits journal topic/scope)
Outcomes: reject, revise-and-resubmit, or accept and publish
After revise-and-resubmit, the author revises based on reviewer comments and it is accepted or rejected
A rejected author may resubmit to another more suitable journal

name: Wakefield vaccines–autism case
q: What does the Wakefield (1998) vaccines–autism case illustrate about scientific literature?
ans:
A poorly-controlled study claimed MMR vaccines were associated with autism
Retracted 12 years later, but the vaccine scare damage was done
Undisclosed conflict of interest: authors paid by lawyers hired by parents of autistic children
Shows why scholarly work must be properly reviewed and vetted before reaching the public

name: What is NOT scientific literature
q: What kinds of sources are NOT considered scientific literature, and why?
ans:
Blog posts, newspaper articles, magazine articles
Wikipedia, WikiHow and other wikis, HowStuffWorks, LiveStrong
They may look scientific but could be written by opinionated experts
Having a PhD is not proof of credibility if the person lacks expertise in that area

name: White/policy papers (grey area)
q: Why are white/policy papers a 'grey area' as sources?
ans:
Reports written by organisations for government policies/purposes
Not peer-reviewed or published in journals/textbooks
May contain research or summaries, so can still be valid and rigorous
May be driven by personal/financial interests; check if the author is credible and non-partisan (e.g. WHO) and the topic is relevant

name: Information literacy
q: What is information literacy and how does it make you a better consumer of information?
ans:
The ability to know what information is needed and to locate, evaluate and effectively use it
Includes distinguishing credible from non-credible sources
Lets you favour evidence-based info and be sceptical of outrageous claims
Be critical even of experts: they disagree, so check different (contradicting) sources and reach your own conclusion

name: Empirical paper as a story
q: How does the 'story' analogy map onto the parts of an empirical paper?
ans:
Interesting topic and similar past stories = literature review
Story is incomplete, predictions made = research gap and hypotheses
How the story was built with data = methods and analysis
What the next part should be = discussion and future research

name: Title and abstract
q: What should the title and the abstract of an empirical paper contain?
ans:
Title: the specific topic of study (e.g. 'Positive emotions trigger upward spirals toward emotional well-being', not just 'Emotions and well-being')
Abstract: a brief 150–250 word summary of the report

name: Introduction / literature review section
q: What does the introduction/literature review section of an empirical paper do?
ans:
Gives background, defines key variables, presents theories and past research
Highlights what has NOT been done and why it SHOULD be done
States aim, theoretical framework, research question, hypotheses and potential contributions
Positions the study in its research area; not always labelled 'introduction'; leads logically to the method

name: Core contents of the introduction
q: What six core contents should an introduction/literature review contain?
clues: Starts with background, ends with contributions
ans:
Background: what the paper is about and why it matters
Literature/past research: relevant variables, definitions, past findings
Theoretical framework: how and why variables are related; informs hypotheses
Research gap: what hasn't been studied and why it should be
Research question and hypotheses
Expected contributions and implications

name: Research gap
q: What is a research gap in an empirical paper?
ans:
The aspects of a research topic that have not yet been studied/examined
Plus why they should be examined
Knowing the gap tells you what question to ask (research question)

name: Theoretical framework
q: What role does the theoretical framework play in an empirical paper's introduction?
ans:
Explains how and why the variables are connected/related
Informs the hypotheses
Presented in the introduction/literature review

name: Method section
q: What four kinds of information should the Method section of an empirical paper provide?
clues: Design, who, how measured, what was done
ans:
General method/approach: design (experiment, survey, longitudinal?)
Sample: who participated, characteristics, inclusion/exclusion
Measures/materials: how variables were measured (operational definitions)
Procedure: what participants did; the manipulation if an experiment
Detailed enough for others to replicate the study

name: Results section
q: What does the Results section of an empirical paper contain?
ans:
Collation of data and a brief description of the data collected
Statistical analyses conducted to test the hypotheses
Whether the data supported or did not support the hypotheses

name: Discussion section
q: What does the Discussion section of an empirical paper contain?
ans:
Non-technical/non-statistical interpretation of results
What results mean for the study and the wider literature
Answer to the research question
Limitations and weaknesses
Suggestions for future studies; theoretical and practical implications

name: Results vs Discussion
q: How does the Results section differ from the Discussion section?
ans:
Results: reports data and statistical analyses; states whether hypotheses were supported
Discussion: non-statistical interpretation, meaning in the wider literature, answer to the research question, limitations, future studies, implications

name: Conceptual definition
q: What is a conceptual definition of a variable?
ans:
Defines the variable according to its meaning/characteristics
E.g. creativity = 'the production of novel, useful products' (Mumford, 2003)
A variable can have several conceptual definitions

name: Operational definition
q: What is an operational definition of a variable?
clues: Found in the Measures part of the Method
ans:
Defines how the variable is measured
E.g. creativity = total score on the Torrance Tests of Creative Thinking (TTCT) or the Creative Achievement Questionnaire (CAQ)
Listed under Measures in the Method section

name: Conceptual vs operational definitions
q: What is the difference between conceptual and operational definitions?
ans:
Conceptual: what the variable means (its characteristics)
Operational: how the variable is measured
E.g. creativity conceptually = production of novel and useful ideas; operationally = total TTCT score

name: Variables (Lecture 2 definition)
q: How does Lecture 2 define variables, using the handedness–creativity example?
clues: Vary in degree, amount or intensity
ans:
Any measurable phenomena that can change (vary) in degree, amount or intensity
Handedness: whether someone is right- or left-handed
Creativity: the extent someone can think up novel or inventive ideas/solutions

name: Research question in an empirical paper
q: What can a research question in an empirical paper specify?
ans:
A specific expected relationship between two specific variables
E.g. Are right-handers more creative than left-handers?
E.g. Does excessive smartphone usage negatively affect satisfaction with life?

name: Hypotheses and how to find them
q: What are an empirical article's hypotheses, and how do you find them when they are not explicitly stated?
ans:
The expected answers to the research question, based on past research evidence
Present predictions of results and how the data are expected to appear
Sometimes listed separately (Hypothesis 1, 2…)
If not explicit (as in Beall & Tracy, 2013), look for 'expect', 'predict', 'hypothesize'

name: Beall & Tracy (2013) practice article
q: What is the Beall and Tracy (2013) article used for in Lecture 2, and what are its variables?
ans:
Practice article for Assignment 1: 'Women are more likely to wear red or pink at peak fertility'
Used to find the research question, hypotheses and methods
Variables: shirt colour and fertility
Its hypotheses are not explicitly stated

name: Theoretical framework (definition)
q: What is the theoretical framework of an empirical study?
clues: Two related words: explain and justify
ans:
The explanations and/or justification for the study's hypotheses
A reasoned explanation of how and why the variables are connected
A rationale for making predictions between two variables

name: Purpose: how and why
q: What two questions should a theoretical framework answer about variables A and B?
ans:
How is A related to B?
Why is A related to B?
It should explain HOW and WHY the variables are connected

name: Convincing the reader
q: In a theoretical framework, what are you trying to convince your reader of?
clues: Why these variables sit in the same study
ans:
Why these variables are being studied together in the same study
What your justification is for studying these variables together

name: Testosterone–aggression example
q: In the lecture's example of a theoretical framework for 'Men are more physically aggressive than women', what is the reasoning?
ans:
High testosterone predicts competitiveness, desire for status and dominance
These translate to greater likelihood of physical aggression
Men have higher testosterone than women
Therefore men are more likely to be physically aggressive

name: Theoretical framework is / is not
q: What is a theoretical framework NOT, according to the lecture?
ans:
Not always explicitly labelled a 'framework' or 'model' (you may need to infer it from a thorough reading)
Not just a summary of past results (that doesn't say how variables relate)
Not the same as a theory (listing a theory without explanation is not a framework)

name: Smartphone–life satisfaction example (set-up)
q: What were the research question and aim in the lecture's smartphone example of forming a theoretical framework?
clues: Background: many people use smartphones yet seem less happy
ans:
RQ: Does excessive smartphone usage negatively relate to satisfaction with one's life?
Aim: to examine if hours of smartphone usage is negatively related to life satisfaction
Hypothesis: negative relationship between hours on the smartphone and satisfaction with life

name: Social comparison processes as framework
q: How do social comparison processes (Festinger, 1954) explain the link between smartphone use and lower life satisfaction?
clues: It's not the phone itself but what people do on it
ans:
It is the actions done through smartphones, not mere use, that lower life satisfaction
People use smartphones for social media, which presents others' lives more favourably
Unfavourable comparisons make one's own life seem less satisfying
They also cause envy and jealousy, which lower life satisfaction

name: Graphical representation of the framework
q: In the graphical representation of the smartphone theoretical framework, which part is the theoretical framework itself?
clues: Not the starting observation or the end claim
ans:
The middle steps linking smartphone use to lower life satisfaction
Using social media leads to unfavourable comparisons with others' lives
These lead to envy, jealousy and dissatisfaction (social comparison theory)
This middle chain must be explained using research evidence

name: Key word: explanation
q: If you remember only one word about the theoretical framework, what should it be, and why?
clues: What the framework does to a relationship
ans:
'Explanation'
The theoretical framework explains the relationship between two variables

name: Water-to-ice example
q: In the 'how does water become ice?' example, which explanation works like a good theoretical framework, and why?
clues: One explains molecules, one just states a threshold
ans:
Explanation 1 (molecules lose energy, slow down and stick together at around 0°C)
It explains the mechanism: HOW and WHY cooling leads to ice
Explanation 2 only states that water turns to ice at 0°C or below, without explaining why

name: Challenge in psychology frameworks
q: What is the added challenge when describing a theoretical framework in most areas of psychology?
ans:
You need to explain how abstract, intangible concepts relate to one another
Except perhaps in biopsychology or neuropsychology

name: Assignment 1: theoretical framework
q: What must you do with the theoretical framework for Assignment 1?
ans:
Identify the theoretical framework in the article (Beall & Tracy, 2013, red/pink at peak fertility)
Describe it in your own words

name: Results section (definition)
q: Where is the Results section of an empirical paper and what does it contain?
ans:
Presented after the Methods section
Details the findings: the outcomes of the statistical tests conducted on the hypotheses
Do not skip it, even if you don't understand the statistics/symbols (α, β, ΔR², r, χ², F, t, p)

name: Why the Results section is important
q: Why is the Results section important to read?
ans:
It is the first section to report whether the hypothesis is supported (look for 'This supports Hypothesis 1')
It gives deeper insight into findings (follow-up/additional tests that test hypotheses more strictly)
It gives details about the strength/magnitude of the effect

name: Effect strength / magnitude
q: Why does the Results section's information on the strength or magnitude of an effect matter?
ans:
Sometimes there is only a very minor difference (effect) or a weak relationship between variables
You want to know how strong the effect of the relationship is

name: Reading Results against the hypothesis
q: What should you always refer to in order to understand the Results section, and why?
clues: Something stated earlier in the paper
ans:
Always refer to the hypothesis
The Results should be written to correspond with the predictions
This lets you answer the research question

name: 'Significant' / statistical significance
q: What does 'significant' usually mean in a Results section?
ans:
It usually implies statistical significance
The observed effect could not have happened by chance

name: p values (p < .05)
q: What does a p value less than .05 (p < .05) mean in a Results section?
ans:
Simple version: the observed effect could not have happened by chance
Correct interpretation: the value is so unlikely that the null should be rejected
Results may also be shown graphically to aid understanding

name: Tip: avoiding the statistics
q: What does the lecture suggest if you feel very uncomfortable reading the Results section?
ans:
Read the literature review, then jump to the Discussion for a description of findings without statistics
You can't avoid statistics forever, so get used to them as soon as you can

name: Four purposes of the Discussion
q: What four purposes does the Discussion section usually serve?
clues: Starts by restating, ends looking ahead
ans:
Summary of results
Links back to broader literature
Implications
Limitations and directions for future research

name: Discussion: summary of results
q: What does the 'summary of results' part of the Discussion do?
ans:
Summarises the key findings of the study
Re-states briefly which hypotheses were supported
(The Discussion is usually easier to read than the Results)

name: Discussion: links back to broader literature
q: What does the 'links back to broader literature' part of the Discussion do?
ans:
Provides a 'big picture' view of the findings
Relates them back to research within the topic area

name: Discussion: limitations and future research
q: What does the 'limitations and directions for future research' part of the Discussion do?
ans:
Acknowledges the limitations and weaknesses of the current study
Suggests what future research should focus on, maybe a new research question

name: Theoretical vs practical implications
q: What is the difference between theoretical and practical implications?
clues: One is about theories, one about the real world
ans:
Theoretical: what findings mean for future research and the advancement of psychological theories
Ask: does the study support, challenge or extend theories? What novel insights does it add?
Practical: what findings mean for the real world (applications)
Ask: who benefits most? How can findings be applied? What recommendations can be offered?

name: Assignment 1: future research
q: What are the rules for the future research suggestion in Assignment 1?
ans:
Assignment 1 focuses on results and suggesting what future research should do
Suggest another study that logically extends/builds on the current findings
It must be your own idea, and you must justify why
Restating the article's own future research suggestion gets ZERO marks for that section

name: Beall & Tracy (2013) practical implications task
q: What questions does the lecture ask you to answer about the practical implications of Beall and Tracy (2013)?
ans:
Who will benefit from understanding that women tend to wear red or pink when ovulating?
How can this knowledge be used for practical purposes?
Also: what future research did the researchers suggest?

name: Why evaluate scientific literature
q: Why should you read scientific articles skeptically and critically?
ans:
All (good) scientists are skeptical and critical of claims made in any research article
As a budding scientist you should be too
Side benefit: you become more critical of non-scientific articles as well

name: Evaluating the Introduction & Literature Review
q: What questions should you ask when evaluating the Introduction and Literature Review?
ans:
Good coverage of directly relevant literature?
Does the theoretical framework justify the hypotheses? Does the evidence support the framework and phenomenon?
Is the research question logical, new and relevant?
Flow and structure: does each point flow naturally to the next?

name: Evaluating the Methods section
q: What questions should you ask when evaluating the Methods section?
ans:
Is it a reasonable, appropriate way to collect data to answer the RQ? Is there a more appropriate way?
Are the measures representative of the variables?
Are the experimental procedures/survey administration unbiased?

name: Evaluating the Results section
q: What questions should you ask when evaluating the Results section?
ans:
What did the authors find? Is it consistent with past research? If not, can they explain why?
Are conclusions and interpretations from the results fair and logical?
Were appropriate statistical analyses used? (advanced)

name: Evaluating the Discussion section
q: What questions should you ask when evaluating the Discussion section?
ans:
Did authors accurately and comprehensively interpret the results?
Did they reference relevant literature and consider alternative explanations?
Were limitations discussed?
Were future research directions suggested?
Were broader practical and/or theoretical implications discussed?

name: Study 1: coffee and alertness
q: In the flawed-study activity, where is the flaw in Study 1 (coffee increases student alertness)?
clues: Compare the results with the hypothesis
ans:
Likely flaw: Results (answer not given on slides)
The non-coffee group spotted more errors, the opposite of the hypothesis
Yet the authors claim 'the hypothesis is supported', an unfair/illogical conclusion

name: Study 2: commitment and motivation
q: In the flawed-study activity, where is the flaw in Study 2 (commitment and motivation)?
ans:
Likely flaw: Methods (answer not given on slides)
The literature is about employees' commitment to their organisation
But the sample was 345 psychology students, so the measures/sample don't represent the variables
(Only the commitment measure is described as reliable and established)

name: Study 3: self-awareness and emotions
q: In the flawed-study activity, where is the flaw in Study 3 (labelling the causes of our emotions)?
clues: What does the literature say about high self-awareness?
Check the direction of the hypothesis
ans:
Likely flaw: Introduction/theoretical framework (answer not given on slides)
The framework says high self-awareness makes people less susceptible to misattribution, implying a positive link with identifying emotions
Yet the RQ and hypothesis predict a negative relationship, so the framework does not justify the hypothesis

name: Study 4: Facebook and trust
q: In the flawed-study activity, what is wrong with Study 4 (Facebook ruins relationships)?
clues: Compare the variable in the RQ and the hypothesis
ans:
Likely flaw: Methods (answer not given on slides)
The hypothesis compares couples who stay off Facebook with those who keep using it, but all 64 couples were measured the same way, with no comparison group
Also, the hypothesis names relationship 'satisfaction' while the RQ, method and results are about trust

name: Academic writing
q: How does Lecture 4 define academic writing?
ans:
The formal and logical expression of intellectual information
A form of professional writing conveying research findings/scholarly discussion clearly, objectively and critically
Objective in tone: represents facts, not opinions or personal feelings
Used in assignments, reports and publications; need not be dry or boring

name: Four characteristics of academic writing
q: What four characteristics does academic (scholarly) writing tend to have?
ans:
Critical
Informed
Intellectual
Objective

name: Mature tone
q: Why does academic writing require a mature tone?
ans:
Conveys maturity and authority, so the writer seems trustworthy and the information accurate and reliable
Your voice shows how well you know your topic
Readers judge how convincing/persuasive you are from your tone

name: High school vs university writing
q: How does writing in high school differ from writing in university according to Lecture 4?
ans:
High school: writing indicates your understanding
University and beyond: writing indicates the quality of your thoughts

name: Formality and audience
q: Who is the typical audience of academic writing, and how does this affect formality?
ans:
Academic writing conveys a degree of formality; tone/style varies by context
Typical audience: researchers, professionals from various industries, professors/lecturers/teachers
NOT your course mates or friends

name: Four qualities of academic writing
q: What four qualities does academic writing typically have?
ans:
Moderate–high lexical density: concise, every word counts
Nominal style: favours nouns over verbs
Impersonal constructions: third-person perspective
Hedging and emphasizing: conveys cautious judgment

name: Lexical density
q: What is lexical density?
ans:
The compactness of language: how economical the writer is with words
High density conveys a lot of information in fewer words
But high density also makes text more specialised/technical

name: Lexical density formula
q: How is lexical density calculated?
ans:
(Number of content/lexical words ÷ total number of words) × 100
Total words = content words + function words
E.g. 'An autistic child is weaker in communication skills compared to a regular child' = 8/13 × 100 = 61.5%

name: Content words vs function words
q: What is the difference between content (lexical) words and function words?
ans:
Content words: nouns, adjectives, verbs, adverbs; any word that carries meaning
Function words: articles, prepositions, conjunctions (e.g. if, then, thus, the, and)
Function words connect words but carry no meaning by themselves

name: Typical lexical density by source
q: What are the typical lexical density ranges for different types of text?
ans:
Expository writing (Wikipedia, newspapers): 55–58%
Fiction, general prose: 48–51%
Interview transcripts, spoken language: about 45%

name: Levels of lexical density
q: What characterises high, moderate, low and very low lexical density texts?
ans:
High: specialised texts, easiest for experts; may sound technical/complex
Moderate: accessible to well-educated non-experts with good vocabulary
Low: understood by most people; conversational
Very low: may seem meaningless, vague or hesitant; excessively verbose

name: High vs low lexical density (example)
q: How does the social support–academic stress example illustrate high vs low lexical density?
ans:
Low (50%): 'As a matter of fact, it has been shown repeatedly that social support is an important predictor of academic stress.'
High (88%): 'Studies show that social support lowers academic stress.'
Same idea, far fewer filler words in the high-density version

name: Concise and jargon-free writing
q: When is high lexical density acceptable, and what does Strunk's 'every word tell' mean?
clues: No unnecessary lines in a drawing
ans:
High density is acceptable if all specialist terms/constructs/variables are clearly defined
Strunk (2000): no unnecessary words in a sentence or sentences in a paragraph
This does not mean all sentences must be short or lack detail, but that every word tell

name: Getting to the point (consent form example)
q: What does the consent form / Stroop test example show about getting to the point?
ans:
Wordy version: 47 words repeating the consent-form steps
Concise version: 18 words ('After signing the consent form, the participants were administered the Stroop test…')
Same information in far fewer words; cut repetition and unnecessary steps
Academic readers want your main point as soon as possible

name: Telegraphing
q: What is 'telegraphing' in writing and what should you do about it?
ans:
Announcing what the text is about to do instead of doing it
E.g. 'This review will show that…', 'This introduction will discuss…', 'This is relevant because…'
These phrases are unnecessary and should be removed

name: Weasel words
q: What are weasel words?
ans:
Ambiguous and misleading phrases to avoid
E.g. 'Many people believe that…'
E.g. 'Researchers generally believe…'

name: Telegraphing vs weasel words
q: What is the difference between telegraphing and weasel words?
ans:
Telegraphing: unnecessary signposting of what the text will do ('This review will show…')
Weasel words: ambiguous/misleading claims with vague sources ('Many people believe…')
Both should be removed to write concisely

name: Nominal style / nominalization
q: What is nominalization (nominal style) and why is it used in academic writing?
clues: Turning one word class into another
ans:
Turning verbs (actions) into nouns (concepts/ideas)
Creates a more convincing and confident tone
E.g. 'The writing of a manuscript necessarily involves matters of time management' vs 'Manuscript writing requires effective time management skills'

name: Verbs vs nouns
q: How does Lecture 4 define verbs and nouns for nominalization?
ans:
Verbs: words describing actions, states or occurrences
Nouns: words describing a class of person, place or thing
Nominalization turns verbs (actions) into nouns (concepts)

name: Nominalization examples
q: How are the teen promiscuity and academic stress sentences nominalized?
ans:
'getting involved in promiscuous behaviour' becomes 'promiscuity'; 'catch and spread STDs' becomes 'sexual health concern'
Result: 'Promiscuity among teens presents a sexual health concern.'
'worry… getting stressed' becomes 'academic stress and worry'; 'have to do a lot of assignments' becomes 'hectic assignment schedule'

name: Impersonal construction
q: What is impersonal construction in academic writing?
ans:
'Backgrounding' the subjects: both participants and the author
Uses passive or third-person perspective
Makes the phenomenon, not the researcher, the focus of the sentence
E.g. 'The questionnaires were then administered to the participants' rather than 'The researcher then handed out the questionnaires'

name: Limiting personal pronouns
q: Why should you limit personal pronouns in academic writing, and when are they acceptable?
clues: I, we, you, me, my, ours, us
ans:
Over-use makes text sound casual: less formal, authoritative and objective
Acceptable if the pronoun improves clarity and brevity
In group research, refer to yourselves as 'the researchers' or 'the research team' instead of 'we/us'

name: Hedging language
q: What is hedging language and what does it show about the writer?
ans:
The use of more cautious language indicating tentativeness of claims/conclusions
Shows the writer is open to revising conclusions with new evidence
Shows the writer acknowledges own bias and potential for inaccuracy
Hedging words: may, possibly, indicates, suggests

name: Words implying certainty
q: Which words implying certainty should academic writers avoid, and why?
ans:
prove, must, fact, definitely, always
They come across as overly strong
They can call your judgment into question

name: Hedged vs overconfident claims
q: How does the social support example contrast a hedged claim with an overconfident claim?
ans:
Overconfident: 'These findings prove that social support will determine how stressed a student is'
Hedged: 'These findings suggest that the level of social support… may predict academic stress'
Hedging terms used: suggest, may (also 'hints', 'might' in the classical music example)
Impersonal construction also adds objectivity

name: Avoiding bias in writing
q: What kinds of bias should be avoided in academic writing, and how can wording be fixed?
ans:
Bias can seem like favouritism or be offensive: sexism, racism, nationalism, religious bias
'50 men and 50 girls' becomes '50 men and 50 women'
'rate… regarding her effectiveness' becomes 'their effectiveness'
'The elderly (50+)' becomes 'participants aged 50 and above'; 'black people' becomes 'African participants'

name: Notes on academic writing
q: What general notes does Lecture 4 give for applying academic writing style?
ans:
Apply nominalization and lexical density sentence by sentence
Re-read for overall flow and tone
Keep a constructive, respectful tone in literature reviews; don't be excessively critical
Avoid informal expressions/contractions (don't, can't, wouldn't)

name: Benefits of reading for writing
q: How does reading broadly help your writing?
ans:
Improves language skills and vocabulary
Exposes you to better writing so you learn by example
Shows good pacing, phrasing and structure
Helps you adopt your own unique author writing voice

name: Reading-for-writing strategies
q: What strategies does Lecture 4 suggest for reading in order to improve writing?
ans:
Read regularly (e.g. an hour a day; books are a good start)
Analyse structure and flow: why did the author say this, here, in this tone?
Compare articles: similarities, differences, what we don't know, possible research gaps
Notice words used and how (if at all) variables are defined

name: Specialized terms vs common usage
q: Why should you be careful with specialized terms in scientific reports, and what should you cite when defining them?
ans:
Terms in scientific reports may mean something different from everyday conversational use
Dictionary definitions are NOT conceptual definitions
So cite an academic article, not a dictionary, when defining terms
Scientific writing uses terms precisely and consistently, giving a fixed label for variables

name: 'Significant' (scientific meaning)
q: What does 'significant' mean in scientific writing, compared with its everyday meaning?
ans:
Everyday: having meaning, or having influence/effect
Closest dictionary sense: probably caused by something other than mere chance
Scientific: a statistically significant difference or relationship between defined variables
As indicated by a valid statistical test (e.g. t-tests, ANOVAs, multiple regression)

name: Validity vs reliability
q: How do validity and reliability differ in scientific reports?
ans:
Validity: use of appropriate procedures, measures or techniques for answering a research question
Reliability: whether the design/measures return consistent results
Everyday 'validity' = well-grounded, sound, or legally acceptable
Everyday 'reliability' = same results on repeated trials

name: Causal language
q: When is causal language (effect, affect, impact, cause, increase, decrease, influence) appropriate?
ans:
Only appropriate for experimental studies
Experiments manipulate one variable to see its effects on another
Only then can you say 'a change in X affects/causes/increases a change in Y'
If the study is not an experiment, avoid any word implying causality

name: Language for correlational studies
q: What wording is appropriate for describing results in non-experimental (correlational) studies?
ans:
'related to…'
'associated with…'
'positive relationship between…'
'negative relationship between…'

name: Language for group comparisons (non-experimental)
q: What wording is appropriate in non-experimental studies that compare groups rather than assess relationships?
ans:
'Difference between…'
'X will be significantly higher than…'
'The average score of Y will be higher than…'

name: Writing as an iterative process
q: What does it mean that writing is an iterative process, and what do good science writers do?
ans:
You write, re-write and re-write until the work is as good as it can or should be
Usually free/rough writing followed by lots of editing
Editing usually takes longer and needs more attention than the initial writing
Good writers assess clarity, flow and structure
Good science writers are ruthless: cut unnecessary detail, elaborate on anything unclear

name: Six steps of the drafting process
q: What are the six steps of the drafting process, in order?
ans:
1 Free writing
2 Develop an outline
3 First draft
4 Redrafting/Revising
5 Editing
6 Polishing

name: Free writing vs developing an outline
q: How does the free writing stage differ from the develop-an-outline stage of drafting?
ans:
Free writing: simply jot down any ideas
List concepts, variables, terms, theories or anything you want mentioned
Outline: list these ideas in a particular order

name: First draft
q: What should you do (and not worry about) during the first draft stage?
ans:
Flesh out the ideas and elaborate on points freely
Don't worry about grammar; don't stop if you can't find the right words
Poor writing > No writing
Don't worry too much about the word limit yet

name: Redrafting/Revising
q: What do you check for during the redrafting/revising stage?
ans:
Re-read and ask whether ideas can be expressed more clearly
Are ideas in an ideal, logical order? (affects flow)
Do some points need more justification/evidence?
Consider who might agree or disagree with your points

name: Editing stage
q: What happens during the editing stage of drafting?
ans:
Sentence-level and paragraph-level changes, incl. rewriting sentences or whole paragraphs
Edit word choice, grammar, order of words/sentences
Keep only what is absolutely necessary; simplify where possible
Avoid fluff – never add material just to raise word count

name: Polishing stage
q: What do you pay attention to in the polishing stage?
ans:
Formatting
Minor spelling and grammar errors (e.g. 'an' vs 'and' – may not be caught by the word processor)
Punctuation
Take a break when proofreading

name: Additional drafting tips
q: What additional tips does the lecture give for rethinking your writing and examining it from the outside?
ans:
Critically examine your arguments: would an objective reader be convinced?
Re-read after taking a break (you can be too close to your work – leave it a day or two)
Get brutally honest feedback from a trusted friend, tutor or classmate
If you don't spot obvious errors, others will

name: Good paragraphing guidelines
q: What are the lecture's guidelines for paragraph length and structure?
ans:
Divide paragraphs by points; one key point per paragraph
Keep them short – usually 3–5 sentences on one point
Single sentences are not paragraphs
No paragraphs = Massive Death Wall of Text (MDWT)

name: One point per paragraph & transitions
q: How should a 'one point per paragraph' paragraph be ordered and linked to the next?
ans:
Limit to one key point per paragraph
Begin with a general statement, then give details
The end of a paragraph should lead to the beginning of the next
Use transition sentences to show connections between paragraphs

name: Sandwich paragraph structure
q: What are the three components of the sandwich paragraph structure?
ans:
Topic sentence: the general point/main idea to elaborate on
Elaboration of point: evidence supporting the topic sentence
Last/concluding sentence: explains relevance to the broader argument and connects to the next idea

name: Piranha sandwich example
q: In the piranha sandwich example, what role does each part of the paragraph play?
ans:
Topic sentence: piranhas are, for the most part, harmless
Elaboration: evidence (Thompson, 2014) that their diet is mainly smaller fish and aquatic plants, not humans
Concluding sentence: emphasizes diet and sets up the next paragraph (e.g. keeping piranhas well-fed)

name: Four considerations in professional correspondence
q: What four things should you consider in professional correspondence?
clues: Who you write to: professors, authors, lecturers
ans:
Formality
Culture
Tone
Goals

name: Importance of corresponding professionally
q: Why is corresponding professionally important, both for you and for your organization?
ans:
For you: recipient more receptive and may reply faster; favourable impression; less misinterpretation (no tone of voice in text)
For your organization: maintains the reputation of those you represent; builds and maintains favourable relationships

name: Degrees of formality spectrum
q: What are the four points on the degrees of formality spectrum, with an example of each?
clues: From friends' texts to legal documents
ans:
Highly informal: texts to a good friend, casual social media
Somewhat informal: messages to colleagues, favours, organizing social events
Somewhat formal: persons-in-charge, supervisors, lecturers, stakeholders, professional contacts
Highly formal: legal documentation, policies and procedures
Professional correspondence is usually moderate–high formality

name: Colloquial features that reduce formality
q: Which colloquial features reduce the formality of correspondence?
ans:
Colloquial = used in ordinary or familiar conversation
Informal greetings (Yo, What's up, Howdy, G'Day, Cheers)
Emphasizing suffixes/words, some culture-specific (-lah, meh, sia, eh, huh)
'Creative' text, emoticons and emojis (??, !!, :D, ^_^)

name: Staying formal until indicated otherwise
q: What tone should you start correspondence in, and when is it acceptable to become less formal?
ans:
Begin in a deferential (respectful) and polite tone using formal titles (Dr., Datuk, Datin, Mr., Mrs., Miss)
Stay formal until indicated otherwise
May change if the recipient prefers first-name address
(Somewhat) okay if the recipient uses an informal tone (e.g. emojis) first

name: Culture: Asian vs Western recipients
q: How does expected formality differ between Asian and Western recipients, and why?
ans:
Asian recipients: very formal – honorifics, acknowledging titles, highly deferential tone
Western recipients: slightly less formal – may sign off with first name only
Due to more egalitarian, low power distance norms in Western cultures
Safest to keep addressing formally – emails may be forwarded

name: Identifying recipient titles and salutations
q: How should you identify and address a recipient's titles in a first professional email?
clues: What if no title can be found?
ans:
Acknowledge their titles – shows you know who they are and take them seriously
Find the proper title: Lecturer, Senior Lecturer, Associate Professor, Professor
Google them; note titles like Datuk, Datin, Tun, Dr. (incl. honorary doctorates)
If unknown: 'Dr.', 'Mr.' or 'Ms.' are safe bets
No formal title: full name or Mr./Ms. [Last Name]

name: Presenting yourself professionally
q: How should you introduce yourself professionally in each of the three correspondence scenarios?
clues: Your own lecturer needs an ID
ans:
No second chance at a first impression (incl. a professional email address)
Outside organization: [Full Name] from [Organization], [Country if overseas]
Within organization: [Full Name] from [Department] at [Organization]
Own lecturer: [Full Name], [Student ID] from [Class/Subject]

name: Stating the purpose concisely
q: What guidelines does the lecture give for stating the purpose of an email concisely?
ans:
Be concise – emails of 75–100 words are most likely to get a response
Effective subject lines are typically under 50 characters
Assume the recipient is very busy and wants to know quickly and clearly what the email is about

name: Formal sign-off
q: What should a formal email sign-off include?
ans:
Preface with 'Yours Sincerely' (or equivalent)
Contact details so the recipient can reach you in several ways
Optionally a professional social media account

name: Literature + Review
q: How does the lecture define 'literature', 'review' and therefore 'literature review'?
clues: Break the term into two words
ans:
Literature: any written works, past findings or existing research on an area of study
Review: an assessment or evaluation, with the intention of instituting change if necessary
Literature review: an assessment or evaluation of existing research, to identify grounds for further research

name: APA definition and purpose of a literature review
q: According to the APA definition, what four things does a literature review do?
ans:
Defines and clarifies the topic or problem
Summarizes previous investigations to show the current state of research
Identifies relations, contradictions, gaps and inconsistencies in the literature
Suggests the next step(s) in addressing the topic or problem

name: Literature review vs mere summary
q: Why is a good literature review more than just a summary of past research?
ans:
It compares and contrasts past research
Aims to suggest new research ideas and possibilities
Includes past research, findings, theories, models and explanations to show what we currently know

name: Four things a good literature review shows
q: What four things do you need to show in a good literature review?
ans:
Definition of variables: clear conceptual definitions
Logical connections between variables: a strong theoretical framework
Evidence: relevant past evidence justifying the framework
Importance: convincing arguments for why more research on the topic matters

name: Five initial stages of conducting a literature review
q: What are the five initial stages of conducting a literature review, in order?
clues: Most of the work happens before writing
Starts with scope, ends with a table
ans:
1 Define your search scope and initial search
2 Quick read
3 Decide on relevance
4 Critical reading
5 Extract and organize
Much of the work is done before any writing, making writing quicker and less stressful

name: Defining your search scope
q: How do you begin defining your search scope for a literature review?
clues: Ask yourself a question about interest
ans:
Ask: what are you interested in?
Interest may come from previous studies or suggestions for future research in an article
Initial search is usually purposefully broad
If you already know your topic, you can start narrow

name: Broad vs narrow initial search
q: What is the difference between a broad and a narrow initial search of the literature?
ans:
Broad: no specific topic yet; review a broad psychology domain (e.g. developmental)
Broad is exploratory – broad but shallow understanding; textbooks help
Narrow: you already know the specific topic (e.g. music therapy for ADHD)
Narrow uses keywords to find research in that area

name: What to identify in a narrow search
q: What aspects of the research can you identify when doing a narrow search?
ans:
Definition and description of the variables
A rough assumption about how the variables may be related
General findings/pattern of results
Commonly used theoretical frameworks/theories
How the variables were measured or manipulated

name: Searching with keywords
q: What are keywords and how do they help an initial literature search?
ans:
Commonly used terms for frequently studied variables in an area
Usually placed after the abstract
Help narrow your search very quickly
E.g. ADHD, attention-deficit hyperactivity disorder, impulse control
A thesaurus and reference lists help find more

name: Using an article's references
q: How can one highly relevant article be used to find more literature?
ans:
Scan its reference list for similar articles
On Google Scholar, click 'Related articles'
Explore the 'Cited by' link

name: Searching topics with limited research
q: What should you do when a topic, like the Fear of Missing Out, has limited research?
ans:
Expand your search area
FOMO = pervasive apprehension that others might be having rewarding experiences from which one is absent (Przybylski et al., 2013)
Besides the article's references, search related terms: feeling left out, social isolation/loneliness, ostracism

name: Quick reading: what each section tells you
q: During a quick reading, what information does each section of an article give you?
ans:
Title: the variables of interest
Abstract: a bird's-eye view of the research in about 150–200 words
Introduction: the general area of research the paper focuses on
Discussion/conclusion: the main take-away of the article

name: Guidelines for deciding relevance
q: What questions help you decide whether an article is relevant to your research topic?
ans:
Are variables similar to how you defined them, conceptually and operationally?
Does it have at least two relevant (or closely related) variables?
Is its theoretical framework relevant to how your variables connect?
Does it have a similar purpose or aim?
Don't be overly strict – set marginal articles aside rather than discard them

name: Closely-related vs broadly-related vs unrelated studies
q: For a topic on music therapy for children with ADHD, how do closely-related, broadly-related and unrelated studies differ?
ans:
A study can be relevant if variables are closely related, even if not identical
Closely related: diagnosis and treatment of ADHD
Broadly related: teacher ratings of hyperactivity, inattentiveness, defiance
Unrelated: identification of children with autism spectrum disorders

name: Active (critical) vs passive reading
q: How does active (critical) reading differ from passive reading?
ans:
Critical reading = active reading: understand the article thoroughly
Pay more attention to specifics of the article
Engage with and critique what you read
Passive reading: only understand the basics or gist

name: Approaching an article critically
q: What guidelines and practical tips help you approach an article critically?
ans:
Keep your research question in mind
Focus on details relevant to it
Ask questions as you read; analyze what you read
Build your own arguments from your reading
Tips: highlight, make notes on the article, bookmark with sticky notes

name: Literature review table
q: What is the purpose of a literature review table?
clues: Final stage of conducting the review
ans:
Organizes everything you have read (extract and organize stage)
Forms an outline to help you write the literature review
Can be built author-centric or concept-centric

name: Author-centric approach
q: What is the author-centric approach to a literature review table, and when should you use it?
ans:
Organize literature by what each study found
Columns like type of paper, hypothesis, method, results (e.g. Kim et al., 2009; Gattino et al., 2011)
Use to dive deep into the specifics of each study, or if new to the topic
Recommended for the second assignment

name: Concept-centric approach
q: What is the concept-centric approach to a literature review table, and when should you use it?
ans:
Organize literature by themes or general findings across studies
Each theme lists sample papers (e.g. music therapy benefits for children with autism)
Use if already familiar with the area and updating on latest findings
Useful for writing review papers

name: Author-centric vs concept-centric
q: How do the author-centric and concept-centric approaches to a literature review table compare?
ans:
Author-centric: organized study by study; deep dive into specifics; suits beginners and Assignment 2
Concept-centric: organized by themes/general findings; suits those familiar with the area and review papers
Both have advantages

name: Important articles
q: How should you treat articles that are especially important to your proposed research?
ans:
They are very closely related to your proposed research area
Some propose methods especially relevant to your research
Single them out and read them critically

name: Stumbling upon new articles
q: What should you do if you stumble upon a new article after you thought you had finished collecting literature?
clues: Or your question is already answered
ans:
New evidence may make you rethink your research question
Or you may find your question has already been answered
In either case you may need to revise your research question

name: Resources for literature reviews
q: Which resources does the lecture recommend for preparing a literature review?
ans:
Scientific/Psychology Report Manual – how to prepare a scientific report, useful up to your thesis
Journal article databases: PsycInfo, EBSCOHost, ScienceDirect, Google Scholar, Academia.edu, ResearchGate, PLoS One

name: Purpose of a literature review
q: What does a literature review aim to persuade the reader of about you as the writer?
ans:
You have read and understood the topic in depth (breadth and depth)
You know the variables and can explain how they connect
You have identified a worthwhile research gap
You can justify the importance of addressing it
In future it can also justify funding your research

name: Qualities of good literature reviews
q: What qualities do good literature reviews share regardless of their structure?
clues: Clarity of terms; attitude of a first-timer
ans:
Arguments flow smoothly and logically from point to point
Little to no ambiguity in how terms are used/defined
Use the sandwich method for paragraphs
First-time writers should be tentative, cautious and humble

name: Broad-narrow-broad approach
q: What happens in each part of the broad-narrow-broad approach to a scientific article?
ans:
Broad opening: introduce the topic, define key terms, give context
Narrow middle: specific research gap, hypotheses, methods, analysis and results
Broad closing: discussion of how results relate back to the topic, limitations, future directions, theoretical and practical implications

name: Broad-narrow-broad for the assignment
q: Which sections of the broad-narrow-broad structure are included in the literature review assignment, and which are left out?
ans:
Include: general introduction; review of existing literature; research gap and research question; focus of current study and hypotheses; theoretical and practical implications
Leave out: method, analysis, results, limitations (no data collected)

name: Writing the top half
q: What goes into the general introduction and the review section when writing the top half of a literature review?
ans:
General introduction: introduce the key topic; highlight why it is important for the current context
Review: define key terms/variables; explain the theoretical framework with evidence; summarize and critique existing evidence
Critique, don't merely summarize
Gradually narrow toward the research gap and question

name: Writing a strong general introduction
q: What makes a strong general introduction to the topic?
clues: Explain it to family and friends
What to avoid in the first sentence
ans:
Clear and relevant; introduce the topic broadly as you would to non-psychologists
Avoid research findings or theory in the first sentence
Tell readers why the topic is relevant to them and why they should keep reading
Show how it influences their lives – statistics help (e.g. '400 million cups of coffee a day')

name: Review of existing literature section
q: What should the review of existing literature section contain?
ans:
The main content: an overview of available literature, detailing articles set aside earlier
Define specialized terms when they are introduced
Explain the theoretical framework – how and why variables are related
Cite relevant articles to support the framework

name: Theoretical framework
q: What is a theoretical framework, and does it need to be a formal theory?
ans:
The explanation for the connections between variables
Does not need to be a formal model or theory
E.g. coffee's rich phytochemistry explains why coffee consumption leads to positive health outcomes
Can be presented via a named model, a concept, or an explanatory mechanism

name: Using multiple theoretical frameworks
q: What does the lecture advise about using multiple theoretical frameworks?
ans:
If using several, state clearly why each was included
Compare and contrast, integrate or combine, and judge each one's validity and strength
Fairly advanced – avoid unless confident
Highly recommended to choose only ONE for a parsimonious explanation

name: Three ways to present a theoretical framework
q: What are the three ways a theoretical framework can be presented, with the lecture's example of each?
clues: A named model, a concept, a mechanism
Video games, Facebook, culture and memory
ans:
Formally named model: General Aggression Model – aggressive games trigger aggressive cognitions, emotions, behaviours
Concept: availability heuristic – heavy Facebook users recall more positive posts and form distorted perceptions of others
Explanatory mechanism: limited processing capacity, priorities shaped by culture, so memories (incl. false memories) reflect cultural values

name: Why cite past research for the framework
q: Why must you cite past research to support your theoretical framework?
ans:
Gives weight to your arguments
Adds continuity and strength
Without it, the framework sounds like personal opinion
Unsupported claims get called into question

name: When past research supports the framework
q: When is a past study relevant for supporting your theoretical framework?
clues: Describing findings alone is not enough
ans:
Explain how the study contributes to the framework, not just what it found
Relevant if it: claims a relationship between the variables
Establishes a direction of causality between them
Explains why the variables are related
Supports or disproves the framework

name: Citation spamming
q: What is citation spamming, and what is the better alternative shown in the lecture?
ans:
Loading sentences with many citations (e.g. many studies on caffeine and heart rate, breathing, wakefulness)
A large number of citations is not an indication of deep reading
Better: cite a focused source, e.g. one meta-analysis (Cano-Marquina et al., 2013) showing wide effects of coffee

name: Include vs exclude when citing a past study
q: What should you include and exclude when describing a past study in a literature review?
ans:
Include: citation and authors; brief description of what they did; key findings (emphasized); brief argument for relevance
Exclude: inferential statistics (e.g. p < .05); detailed procedures or measures; the past study's own theoretical/practical implications

name: Research gap
q: What is a research gap, and how is one illustrated in the coffee example?
clues: Not yet addressed, but should be
ans:
An area of study that has not yet been addressed – but should be
Derived after reviewing the literature, leading to a research question
Coffee: limited evidence on individual (personality) differences in coffee consumption
E.g. caffeine enhances working memory for extraverts but not introverts (Smillie & Gökçen, 2010)

name: Strong vs moderate vs weak research gaps
q: How do strong, moderate and weak research gaps differ?
ans:
Strong: novel, intriguing, addresses an obvious, important gap; may help create a new model/framework
Moderate: replication and logical extension of the lead paper, or compares two competing methods/models
Weak: minimal potential to add/challenge understanding; just a future-research suggestion already in the lead article

name: Research gap pitfalls to avoid
q: What must you avoid when identifying a research gap?
ans:
Identifying gaps you have no intention of addressing
Naming limitations of past studies and doing nothing about them
Claiming your study merely improves on method
Not enough: same study with larger/different sample, different gender/age, or a Malaysian sample

name: Arguing for the research question
q: How should you argue convincingly that your research question needs to be addressed?
ans:
Link evidence step by step to the question
E.g. extraverts benefit more cognitively from caffeine (Lara, 2015); cognitive performance relates to later health literacy (Federman et al., 2009)
So ask: do extraverted coffee drinkers have better long-term health than introverted ones?
State why answers matter (practical dietary implications)

name: Expected theoretical implications
q: What are expected theoretical implications, and what questions help you write them?
clues: Four ways a study can contribute
ans:
The 'so-what' for our understanding of theory or phenomena; why other researchers should take note
Can be briefly stated at the end of the literature review
Ask if the study: advances understanding of theory; contributes to revising theory or challenges findings
Improves understanding of how variables relate; adds nuances/dimensions to theories or models

name: Weak vs strong theoretical implications
q: How do weak and strong expected theoretical implications differ?
ans:
Weak/mediocre: only says findings 'add new understanding to the literature'
Strong: go one step further – refine or extend existing theories
Provide foundations for new theory or models
E.g. linking to Jones and Lejuez (2005) on caffeine and sensation seeking

name: Expected practical implications
q: What are expected practical implications, and what are the do's and don'ts for writing them?
ans:
The 'so-what' for the real world – why non-researchers, decision makers and society should care
Think about usefulness to society, organizations, practitioners, populations; resulting treatments/interventions
Do: be specific to your study; link logically to your theoretical framework
Don't: be overly broad/vague; propose unfeasible or overly grand implications

name: Vague vs specific practical implications
q: What distinguishes a vague practical implication from a specific and thoughtful one in the coffee example?
ans:
Vague: only says it will 'contribute knowledge' so people know coffee affects health – obvious, fits any coffee study
Specific: proposes evidence-based dietary suggestions adjusting coffee intake by personality (e.g. extraverts vs introverts)
Specific states a clear application to people's personalities and food/drink intake

name: Linking implications to the SDGs
q: How can the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) be used when writing expected practical implications?
ans:
The UN's 17 SDGs promote global well-being, sustainability and social development
Consider how your research aim/contribution aligns with an SDG
Shows broader societal relevance and impact of psychological research
Your study need not solve an SDG – small contributions matter
E.g. personality-based diet study aligns with SDG 3 (Good Health and Well-Being)

name: Psychology fields and SDGs
q: How do fields of psychology relate to the SDGs, according to the lecture's example?
ans:
Some SDGs connect more directly to specific fields (e.g. health/clinical/counselling/positive psychology; educational; social; I/O)
Psychology can still contribute to other SDGs
E.g. Russell et al. (2017): negative emotions and habits linked to food waste – relates to SDG 12

name: Literature review outline and tree diagram
q: How does a literature review outline (with a tree diagram) help you write?
clues: Positions points relative to each other
ans:
Helps you write efficiently, position points and refine arguments
Organizes a coherent, logical, well-supported review; lets you edit or discard irrelevant points
Most helpful for the broad parts: introduction and review of literature
Tree diagram first, then point form under headers (e.g. Introduction: consumption rates, coffee trade; Review: debate, phytochemistry, effects)

name: Assessing the flow of an outline
q: What questions should you ask when assessing the flow of your literature review outline?
clues: Do it before writing, as a group
ans:
Does the flow of points make sense?
Are any parts out of place (irrelevant) or better placed elsewhere?
Would someone ask 'Why is this here?' or 'What was the point of this?'

name: Integrity in scientific writing
q: What does integrity in scientific writing mean, and how do we practise it?
clues: It is about other people's ideas
Two skills this lecture focuses on
ans:
Fully and properly acknowledging others' ideas
Practised by using correct citations and paraphrasing
Doing so helps us avoid plagiarizing another's work

name: Paraphrasing
q: What is paraphrasing?
ans:
Using your own words to interpret important information and ideas from someone else's work
Expressing another's ideas in your own words
Still requires a citation to the source

name: Citation
q: What is a citation?
ans:
To refer to, mention or give credit to an idea that is not yours
Acknowledges the idea is not yours
Tells readers where the idea originated from

name: Plagiarism
q: What is plagiarism, and can it be unintentional?
ans:
Copying or stating another's ideas without giving due credit
Mentioning ideas or claims without a citation
Can be either deliberate or accidental

name: Why we cite
q: What two things does citing tell your readers?
ans:
That you are not making things up
Where to refer to for more information about a claim

name: Importance of paraphrasing
q: Why is paraphrasing considered a key skill in academic and professional careers?
clues: What does it show about you?
ans:
You need to express others' ideas in your own words when writing
It demonstrates comprehension of the source material
It demonstrates acknowledgement of the source material

name: Why plagiarism matters
q: Why is plagiarism treated as severe academic and professional misconduct?
ans:
Poor paraphrasing reflects carelessness or outright dishonesty
It is a breach of trust
It reflects poorly on your character and your organization
It disregards others' hard-earned work
In academia it takes marks for others' work and gains an unfair advantage over honest students

name: What counts as plagiarism
q: What actions will lead to suspicions of plagiarism?
ans:
Copying three or more words in a sequence without a citation
Making only minor changes (changing a few words, using synonyms, switching clause/paragraph order)
Copying the structure of presentation from the source
Not citing the source of the original material
Anything uncited is assumed original; if shown otherwise, you can be accused

name: RAP strategy
q: What are the three steps of the RAP strategy for paraphrasing?
ans:
R: Read the original paragraph
A: Ask for the main idea and the evidence supporting it
P: Put it in your own words (do not reproduce the original structure)
Research suggests RAP improves recall from 48% to 84% (Schumaker, 1984)

name: Generation effect
q: What is the Generation Effect and how does it relate to paraphrasing?
ans:
We remember things better if we were the source of that information
Explains why paraphrasing improves comprehension
Restating ideas in your own words makes you the generator

name: How paraphrasing improves comprehension
q: How does paraphrasing improve comprehension, and what happens without comprehension?
ans:
You make the effort to concentrate, read and identify the author's main ideas
You re-state the ideas in sentences that make sense to you
Without comprehension we merely parrot/mimic others' ideas
We may even misinterpret another's ideas

name: Good vs bad paraphrase
q: What distinguishes a good paraphrase from a bad one?
clues: Compare the three Shidlo and Schroeder attempts
ans:
Bad: swaps a few words or names but keeps the original sentence structure (and may lack a citation)
Weak: cited but still follows the original's structure closely
Good: own structure and wording, captures the main idea, adds interpretation, and is cited
A good paraphrase retains the original meaning

name: APA formatting
q: What is APA formatting, and what other styles is it distinguished from?
ans:
Standards of manuscript formatting and presentation prescribed by the American Psychological Association
Ensures consistency and uniformity in presenting scientific papers
Differs from MLA, Harvard Referencing Style, and Chicago Manual of Style

name: General stylistic guidelines
q: What are the APA general stylistic guidelines for a manuscript?
ans:
Double spacing
1-inch (2.54 cm) margins all along the document
Times New Roman, 12 pt

name: APA header levels
q: How are the five APA header levels formatted?
clues: Centered vs flush left vs indented
ans:
Level 1: Centered, Boldface, Title Case; paragraph begins below
Level 2: Flush Left, Boldface, Title Case; paragraph begins below
Level 3: Flush Left, Boldface Italic, Title Case
Level 4: Indented, Boldface, Title Case, ending with a period; paragraph continues on the same line
Level 5: as Level 4 but Boldface Italic

name: Introduction heading rule
q: What heading should the introduction of an APA paper have?
ans:
Do not use a generic 'Introduction' header (unless explicitly asked)
Use the chosen title of the paper instead
The first header within the introduction should be a Level 2 header

name: APA tables
q: What are the APA rules for tables?
ans:
No vertical lines
p-values to three decimal places (e.g., p = .624)
Other values to two decimal places (e.g., M = 4.25, SD = 6.43)
Table titles go above the table

name: APA figures
q: What are the APA rules for figures?
ans:
Most statistical output (graphs) can be simple line drawings
Legends go at the top or to the right of the main figure
Figure titles go above the figure

name: Parenthetical vs narrative citation
q: What is the difference between a parenthetical and a narrative in-text citation?
clues: Which joining word or symbol is used
ans:
Parenthetical: names and year inside brackets, e.g., (Christian & Griffiths, 2016)
Narrative: names part of the sentence, year in brackets, e.g., Christian and Griffiths (2016)
Use '&' inside brackets, 'and' in narrative
Choice depends on sentence structure

name: Author names in citations
q: Whose names and which part of the name go into an APA in-text citation for one or two authors?
ans:
Always cite the authors' surnames (last/family names)
One author: Fredrickson (2004) or (Fredrickson, 2004)
Two authors: name both every time, e.g., (Christian & Griffiths, 2016)

name: Et al. rule (3+ authors)
q: How do you cite a source with more than two authors in APA (current edition)?
ans:
Shorten every citation, including the first, to first author + 'et al.'
E.g., Fredrickson et al. (2003) or (Fredrickson et al., 2003)
Listing all authors on first mention is APA 6th edition and no longer accepted

name: Primary vs secondary citation
q: What is the difference between a primary citation and a secondary citation?
clues: 'Author A says that Author B says...'
ans:
Primary: citing the original source you read first-hand ('this author claims that...')
Secondary: citing Author B as described in Author A's article without reading Author B's article
Use primary citations whenever possible
Only use secondary citations if you really cannot find the source article

name: Secondary citation format
q: How do you format a secondary citation, and what does it imply?
ans:
Original source, then 'as cited in', then the source you read
E.g., (Henderlong & Lepper, 2002, as cited in Brummelman et al., 2004)
Implies you only read the second source (Brummelman et al.)

name: Secondary references and tertiary citations
q: What is allowed and not allowed for secondary sources in the reference list, and what about tertiary citations?
ans:
Secondary citations may be used in text, but not secondary references
Do not include secondary references in the reference list
Never use tertiary citations (X as cited in Y as cited in Z)
Tertiary citations are messy, confusing and likely to misinterpret the original claim

name: Multiple citations of the same source
q: How should you refer again to the same study within a passage?
ans:
You do not have to repeat all the authors' names each time
When it is clear you mean the same study, use 'the authors', 'they', 'their first study'
E.g., Brummelman et al. (2013)... The authors conducted three studies...

name: Citing two or more sources
q: What are the two rules for citing two or more sources together?
ans:
List references in alphabetical order
Separate each reference with a semicolon (;)
E.g., (Henderlong & Lepper, 2002; McKay & Fanning, 2000)
Useful when sources support the same point or to summarize an area of research

name: Same author, same year
q: How do you distinguish two articles by the same author published in the same year?
ans:
Add a letter suffix (a, b, c) after the year
Arrange alphabetically as per your reference list
E.g., Fredrickson (2013a) and Fredrickson (2013b)

name: Direct quote rules
q: What are the APA rules for using a direct quote?
ans:
Use quotation marks around the exact words
Use the usual author surname and year citation
Give the page number, e.g., (Ng, 2017, p. 57) or Haldeman (1994, p. 221)
Limit quotes to no more than 10% of your total work; over-use risks plagiarism
