name: When to use direct quotes
q: When is it ideal to use a direct quotation instead of a paraphrase?
ans:
When presenting an author's position/theory and you want to critique its wording
When paraphrasing may lose or misinterpret the intended idea
When appealing to the author's authority
When giving an accurate word-for-word definition of a construct, term or variable

name: Editing direct quotes
q: How do you show that a direct quote has been altered or shortened?
ans:
Square brackets [ ] mark text changed so it reads grammatically
Three full stops (...) mark that original text has been shortened (truncated)
Only minor edits are allowed

name: Reference list vs bibliography
q: What is the difference between a reference list and a bibliography?
ans:
Reference list: all references cited in your written text (your primary citations)
Bibliography: all materials read in order to write your text
They are not to be confused

name: Reference list formatting rules
q: What are the formatting rules for an APA reference list?
ans:
Start immediately after the article (after the concluding paragraph), on a new page
Arrange entries in alphabetical order
Use a hanging indentation for every entry
Double line spacing
Cross-check against your in-text citations

name: Journal article reference format
q: What is the APA reference format for a journal article?
ans:
Author(s). (Year). Title of article. Journal Name, volume(issue), page range. DOI
Article title: capitalize first word only
Journal name in italics and Title Case; volume in italics
Comma after the first author's initials before '&'
DOI presented as a hyperlink

name: Book vs book chapter reference format
q: How does the APA reference format for a book differ from that for a book chapter?
ans:
Book: Author(s). (Year). Title of book. Publisher. DOI (if available)
Chapter: Author, A. (Year). Title of chapter. In B. Editor (Ed.), Title of book (pp. xx-xx). Publisher. DOI (if available)
Chapter entries add 'In' + editors (Ed./Eds.) and the chapter's page range
Use a chapter entry when a text has chapters by different authors and you cite one

name: DOI
q: What is a DOI, where is it found, and what if an article has none?
ans:
Digital object identifier: a unique numerical identifier for online documents
Usually at the top or bottom of an article's first page; doi.org can look it up
No DOI, retrieved from a non-database website: give the URL as a hyperlink
No DOI, from a journal website or hardcopy only: end the entry at the page numbers

name: Logic
q: How does the lecture define logic?
ans:
The study of correct and incorrect forms of reasoning
Involves assessing the accuracy and relevance of evidence supporting your claims
The basis for thinking and arguing scientifically

name: Being 'reasonable'
q: What does it mean for something to be 'reasonable' in the logical sense?
ans:
Something has supporting evidence
Implies a logical and coherent structure
Our assertions make sense

name: Argument (what it is and is not)
q: What is an argument, and what is it not?
ans:
A statement in which you give people a reason for believing what you said
Shows WHAT is true and WHY it is true
NOT a verbal fight or shouting match

name: Reasons we argue
q: What are the four reasons we argue, according to the lecture?
clues: Funding, meetings, lunch, the family car
ans:
To persuade (e.g., getting research funds)
To give reasons or explanations (e.g., why peers should attend meetings)
To come to a compromise (e.g., deciding on lunch)
To be clearly understood, and to understand others (e.g., borrowing the family car)

name: Logic vs relevance (convincing arguments)
q: What two bases make an argument convincing, and what question does each ask?
clues: One is about acceptance of statements, one about the conclusion
ans:
Logic: are you justified in accepting the statements, and do they link from one to the other?
Relevance: does the conclusion follow from the statements made?
An argument like 'Because I'm your father and I said no!' is not convincing

name: Proposition
q: What is a proposition?
ans:
A sentence that can be either true or false
Arguments consist of a series of propositions
Within an argument a proposition is either a premise or a conclusion

name: Premise vs conclusion
q: What is the difference between a premise and a conclusion?
ans:
Premises: the reasons to believe the conclusion
Conclusion: the claim/perspective you are making or defending
Both are propositions (can be true or false)

name: Identifying propositions
q: How do you decide whether a sentence such as 'Woof!' or 'Hypnosis is a controversial form of therapy' is a proposition?
ans:
Ask whether it makes a claim that can be shown to be true or false
'Hypnosis is a controversial form of therapy' and 'Education should be free for everyone' are propositions
'Woof!', 'Good for you!' and 'This bowl of pumpkin soup' are not: no claim is made

name: Standard form of an argument
q: What is the standard form of an argument and why use it?
ans:
Premise 1, Premise 2 (add premises as necessary), a line, then the Conclusion
Presents propositions logically
Shows how the premises support the conclusion
E.g., The sun is highest at noon / It is noon / So the sun is currently at its highest point

name: Arguments in natural language
q: How do arguments in natural language differ from standard form?
ans:
In daily speech the conclusion can come before the premises
Premises first: 'Since Amy always drinks coffee in the morning, she will be drinking coffee...'
Conclusion first: 'Amy will be drinking coffee..., because she always drinks coffee in the morning'
We often make arguments without realizing it

name: Deductive argument
q: What is a deductive argument?
clues: Kind of truth it aims for
ans:
A series of propositions reasoning from one or more premises to a logically-certain conclusion
Concerned with guaranteed truth
Quality judged by validity and soundness
One of the two forms of argument in the course (the other is inductive)

name: Validity
q: When is a deductive argument valid?
clues: Think of a situation that is impossible
ans:
When it is not possible for all premises to be true AND the conclusion false at the same time
If the premises are true, the conclusion must be true
If the conclusion could be false with true premises, it is not valid
Validity concerns structure, not the factual truth of the claims

name: Venn diagrams for validity
q: How can Venn diagrams be used to test the validity of a deductive argument?
ans:
Draw circles for the categories in the premises (e.g., women, did give birth)
Place the subject (e.g., Alex) where the premises require
If the subject could sit in a region that makes the conclusion false, the argument is invalid
Some arguments need more than two circles

name: Alex gave birth: valid vs invalid
q: Why is 'Only women can give birth; Alex gave birth; so Alex is a woman' valid, but 'Only women can give birth; Alex is a woman; so Alex gave birth' invalid?
ans:
First: anyone who gave birth must be in the women circle, so the conclusion cannot be false
Second: Alex could be a woman who did not give birth
So the second conclusion may be false even if the premises are true: invalid

name: 'Some roses are pink' argument
q: Why is 'All roses are flowers; some flowers are pink; therefore some roses are pink' invalid?
ans:
The pink flowers might not include any roses
The premises do not force the roses circle to overlap the pink circle
We judge only whether the conclusion logically follows, not whether pink roses actually exist

name: Soundness
q: When is a deductive argument sound?
ans:
When the argument's form is valid AND all its premises are actually true
Soundness is the second criterion for a good deductive argument
An invalid argument is automatically unsound

name: Validity: necessary but insufficient
q: Why is validity described as necessary but insufficient for a good argument?
ans:
Validity is the essential first criterion for a good deductive argument
But a valid argument can still have false premises
Soundness (true premises) is also needed
Valid but silly arguments are possible, but usually not sound

name: Three outcomes: invalid, valid-unsound, valid-sound
q: What can be said about an argument that is (a) invalid, (b) valid but unsound, (c) valid and sound?
ans:
Invalid: automatically unsound; a bad or nonsensical argument
Valid but unsound: structurally fine but not necessarily convincing
Valid and sound: structurally fine and convincing (a good argument)

name: Validity vs soundness
q: What is the difference between validity and soundness?
ans:
Validity is about form: the conclusion must follow if the premises are true
Soundness adds that all premises are actually true
'Israel is the capital of New Zealand; Amy is visiting Israel; so Amy is in New Zealand' is valid but unsound
Replacing Israel with Wellington makes it valid and sound

name: Affirming the consequent
q: What is the fallacy of affirming the consequent?
ans:
Form: If P then Q; Q; therefore P
E.g., If it rains, the game is cancelled; the game is cancelled; so it rained
Invalid: Q could have other causes (haze, power outage, viral outbreak)
Being invalid, it is automatically unsound

name: True conclusion, bad argument
q: Can a deductive argument with a true conclusion still be a bad argument?
ans:
Yes: the conclusion must follow from the premises
E.g., Santa's elves travel east to west; Santa controls the sun; so the sun rises in the east
Conclusion is true, but premises give no reason to believe it
Such an argument is invalid and unsound

name: Believability bias
q: What is the believability bias, and how does deductive logic help avoid it?
ans:
Accepting an argument because it sounds believable although its form is invalid
Understanding validity helps us check whether the conclusion follows from the premises

name: Value of deductive logic in psychology
q: If psychology has few absolutes, what is the value of deductive logic?
ans:
Hard sciences (chemistry, physics, biology) can have valid and sound arguments, even theorems
Psychology has few absolutes in human behaviour
Deductive logic still helps us structure good arguments and avoid bad ones
It answers: does the conclusion follow from the premises?

name: Coffee and memory invalid argument
q: Why is 'Coffee drinkers have better memory; our participants showed better memory; so our participants drank coffee' a bad argument?
clues: Same shape as the game-cancelled example
ans:
It is invalid: better memory may have causes other than coffee
Shares the form of affirming the consequent
Because it is invalid, it is automatically unsound

name: Deductive vs inductive logic (preview)
q: How does deductive logic differ from the inductive logic previewed for the next lecture?
ans:
Deductive: aims at guaranteed truth / logically-certain conclusions
Inductive: tells us the degree to which we should believe an argument, since psychology can't guarantee absolute truth
Inductive logic links to generalization, a goal of scientific research

name: To argue
q: What does it mean to argue, in argumentative logic?
clues: The target is a claim or belief
ans: To give reasons to believe a statement, claim, or belief

name: Validity vs soundness
q: How are deductive arguments assessed in terms of validity vs soundness?
clues: One is about the premises' content
ans:
Validity = structural correctness of the argument
Soundness = truth of the premises
Deductive arguments are judged on both

name: Deductive argument
q: What is a deductive argument and what does it aim for?
ans:
A series of propositions reasoning from one or more premises to a logically-certain conclusion
Aims for certainty: a 100% guaranteed true conclusion
All-or-nothing
Few things in human experience can be guaranteed with absolute certainty

name: Inductive argument
q: What is an inductive argument?
ans:
A series of propositions reasoning from one or more premises to a probable conclusion
Not concerned with absolute truth
Gives evidence/statements showing the conclusion is likely
Lets us state a very plausible, very likely conclusion

name: Deductive vs inductive arguments
q: How do deductive vs inductive arguments differ?
ans:
Deductive: logically-certain conclusion; all-or-nothing
Inductive: probable conclusion; continuum of strength
Deductive judged by validity/soundness; inductive by strength
Sun-rising example: cannot be certain, but highly likely

name: Inductive arguments are invalid
q: Why are all inductive arguments considered invalid?
clues: Can true premises give a false conclusion?
They don't try to prove absolute truth
ans:
They are not concerned with absolute truth
All premises can be true while the conclusion is false
e.g. Amy could still place 1st despite the premises

name: Three characteristics of inductive arguments
q: What are the three characteristics of inductive arguments?
ans:
Invalid
Defeasible
Vary in strength

name: Defeasible
q: What does it mean that inductive arguments are defeasible?
ans:
Open to revision, objection or annulment (elimination)
You can add or remove premises to the argument

name: Vary in strength
q: What does it mean that inductive arguments vary in strength?
ans:
Because they can be revised, their strength can change
Adding/removing premises can turn a weak argument strong, or vice versa

name: Strengthening vs weakening a conclusion (Amy example)
q: In the Amy marathon example, what is the difference between strengthening vs weakening the conclusion?
clues: The conclusion is that Amy is unlikely to place 1st
Which direction makes her win more likely?
ans:
Conclusion: Amy is very unlikely to place 1st
Weakening premises make it more likely Amy places 1st
Strengthening premises make it more likely Amy loses
The argument is invalid but can vary in strength

name: Criteria for a strong premise
q: What three criteria determine whether a premise added to an inductive argument is strong?
ans:
True: based in truth, fact and/or reality
Justified: there is evidence to back it
Relevant: it bears on the conclusion
Meeting all three = a strong premise; also consider context and stakes

name: Context of an argument
q: What is the context of an inductive argument?
clues: Wine example: Friday night vs doctor's advice
ans:
The situation/circumstance in which the inductive argument is made
e.g. drinking wine because others are (less important) vs because a doctor recommended a Mediterranean diet (more important)

name: Stakes of an argument
q: What are the stakes of an inductive argument?
ans:
The potential impact of the conclusion following from the inductive argument
Stakes are higher when e.g. a doctor prescribed the diet
Stakes are lower if there is no evidence for the health benefit

name: Context vs stakes
q: How does the context of an argument differ from its stakes?
clues: Both affect how premises are judged
ans:
Context = the situation/circumstance in which the argument is made
Stakes = the potential impact of the conclusion
Both should be considered when adding/challenging premises (e.g. human rights debates)

name: Generalizing
q: What does generalizing mean in the psychological sciences?
ans:
Observing characteristics/behavioural tendencies in a small group of people
Then arguing that others like that group will share them
Inductive arguments are useful for generalizing, though not certain

name: Swan generalization
q: Why is the white-swan argument a poor generalization?
ans:
Premises: I have seen 100 swans; every one was white
Conclusion: it is likely all swans are white
Extends a small sample to all swans, including those never seen
Obviously not a good generalization

name: Criteria for strong generalizations
q: What three criteria make generalizations stronger?
ans:
Logic: premises justified, relevant and/or true; conclusion flows from premises
Sample size: is the sample large enough?
Objectivity: is the sample or data collection biased?

name: Objectivity (generalization criterion)
q: What does the objectivity criterion for generalizations ask?
ans:
Is the sample biased?
Was the approach to data collection biased in any way?

name: Applying generalizations to specific cases
q: Why are generalizations only useful if we can apply them back to specific cases?
ans:
A main goal of psychological research is to apply findings from a small study to a larger population
e.g. St. John's Wort (23 trials), mindfulness meta-analysis (39 studies), extraversion/agreeableness and well-being (148 studies)

name: Falsifiability
q: What is falsifiability in science?
ans:
A premise must be falsifiable in science
Asks: can the proposition be proven wrong?
If a claim cannot be proven true or otherwise, it is not reasonable to accept it

name: Invisible dragon example
q: What does the invisible dragon example illustrate?
ans:
The dragon is invisible, weightless, odourless and cannot be touched
No test could show it exists or not
An unfalsifiable claim is not reasonable to accept

name: Unfalsifiable claims (Activity 5)
q: What makes claims like the 'repressed memory' or 'vegans are in denial' statements unfalsifiable?
ans:
Any counter-evidence is explained away (denial = repression/denial; contrary data = flawed)
So no conceivable event could prove them wrong
Contrast: 'the sun rises in the east' can be tested

name: Falsification (how science progresses)
q: How does science progress through falsification?
clues: What to believe and what not to
ans:
Bad ideas, inaccurate theories or flawed findings are eliminated
What remains is closer to the truth
Research tells us what to believe and what not to believe

name: Karl Popper's view
q: What did Karl Popper (1963) argue about confirmation and refutability?
ans:
Confirmations are easy to find for nearly any theory if we look for them
A theory not refutable by any conceivable event is non-scientific
Irrefutability is a vice, not a virtue
Every genuine test of a theory is an attempt to falsify it

name: Progress through falsifiability
q: What happens to a theory under progress through falsifiability?
ans:
A more stringent test: how much evidence goes against the theory
Much support, little disproof: retain it as a good representation of reality
New challenging evidence: revise or discard it
e.g. left/right brain, handwriting, skull bumps, blood-type personality were discarded

name: White swans vs non-white swans
q: In the swan argument, should you look for more white swans or non-white swans, and why?
ans:
Look for non-white swans
Confirmations are easy to find
A genuine test tries to falsify the generalization

name: Fallacy
q: What is a fallacy in argumentative logic?
ans:
A failure in reasoning that renders an argument invalid
Premises are presented as supporting the conclusion when in reality they do not
Everyone makes fallacious arguments

name: Types of logical fallacies
q: What types of logical fallacies are covered in the lecture?
ans:
Slippery slope; false dichotomy; ambiguity
Fallacies of relevance (ad hominem, appeal to authority, popular assent)
Circular arguments; straw man; red herring; false equivalence

name: Slippery slope
q: What is the slippery slope fallacy?
ans:
Asserting that a course of action will lead to an unwanted, bad or disastrous outcome
Format: if you allow x, the terrible y will happen!
Fallacy: there is no evidence the bad consequence will happen

name: False dichotomy
q: What is the false dichotomy fallacy?
ans:
Proposing that there are only two possibilities
Format: we only have two choices, x or y
Fallacy: no evidence there are only two options/outcomes

name: Ambiguity
q: What is the fallacy of ambiguity?
ans:
Phrasing an argument so it has more than one acceptable interpretation
No specific format; depends on the words used
Switching between interpretations leads to faulty conclusions
e.g. 'a feather is light; light things are not dark; so no dark feathers'

name: Vagueness (when acceptable)
q: When is vagueness acceptable, according to the note on ambiguity?
ans:
Natural language contains hard-to-avoid vagueness
Acceptable when we lack full information, e.g. 'I'll visit the US sometime next year'
Not deliberately misleading
Should be avoided for factual claims in high-stakes situations

name: Fallacies of relevance (non sequitur)
q: What is a fallacy of relevance?
ans:
Proposing a premise irrelevant to supporting the conclusion (a 'non sequitur')
Format: we should/should not believe x because <irrelevant point>
The conclusion does not follow from the premises
Invalid for deductive arguments; weak for inductive arguments

name: Three forms of fallacies of relevance
q: What are the three main forms of fallacies of relevance?
ans:
Ad hominem
Appeal to authority
Appeal to popular assent
Other irrelevant appeals: appeals to emotion and tradition

name: Ad hominem
q: What is the ad hominem fallacy?
ans:
Attacking the person instead of giving a reason about the argument
Targets their entitlement to speak, their premises or their conclusions
Format: we should not believe x because person y is not entitled / uses bad reasons / gives bad conclusions

name: Three targets of ad hominem
q: What three things can an ad hominem attack target (Cooper example)?
ans:
Entitlement to speak: 'never been in a relationship, so not qualified'
Reasons/premises: 'his reasons are just theories'
Conclusions: 'anything he concludes is not believable'

name: Legitimate credibility concerns vs ad hominem
q: When is questioning a person's credibility legitimate rather than an ad hominem fallacy?
ans:
When we have good reasons, e.g. concerns about authority/expertise
Or suspected conflicts of interest affecting truth claims
But a well-supported argument should not be dismissed simply because of who the person is

name: Appeal to authority
q: What is the appeal to authority fallacy?
ans:
Supporting an argument because it is made by someone with authority or expertise
Format: we should believe x because person y is entitled / uses good reasons / gives good conclusions
Uses the speaker's credibility to claim the conclusion is true
Opposite of ad hominem

name: Ad hominem vs appeal to authority
q: How does ad hominem differ from appeal to authority?
ans:
Ad hominem: reject x because of who the person is
Appeal to authority: accept x because of who the person is
Both rest on the person, not the argument

name: Appeal to popular assent
q: What is the appeal to popular assent fallacy?
ans:
Supporting an argument because the majority agrees (or disagrees) with it
Format: we should believe x because most people / a large sample / everyone believes x
Fallacy: majority belief does not make it true

name: Appeal to authority vs popular assent
q: How does an appeal to authority differ from an appeal to popular assent?
ans:
Authority: endorse x because an expert/authority holds it
Popular assent: endorse x because the majority holds it
Both treat who believes x as proof x is true

name: Appeal to emotion
q: What is an appeal to emotion?
ans:
A fallacy of relevance appealing to another person's emotions, such as guilt or pity
e.g. 'If we find this boy guilty, his life will be in ruins!'

name: Appeal to tradition
q: What is an appeal to tradition?
ans:
A fallacy of relevance: 'this is how it's always been done, why fix it?'
e.g. 'We have always celebrated Thanksgiving together; you can't break that tradition'

name: Circular argument
q: What is a circular argument?
ans:
The premises contain the conclusion
Format: A implies B, which implies A...
Or assuming what we are trying to prove
e.g. 'Ban intoxicating beverages because they make people drunk'

name: Straw man
q: What is a straw man argument?
ans:
Wilfully misrepresenting the argument we want to refute, then arguing against that misrepresentation
Usually appears in responses to others' arguments
Format: 'So you're saying y?'
e.g. free birth control/safe sex recast as encouraging promiscuity

name: Red herring
q: What is a red herring fallacy?
ans:
Diverting attention from the topic by introducing another topic (a distractor)
Most evident in responses to the other person
Format: 'Yes, but let's think about y...'
e.g. responding to 'cheating is wrong' by debating what morality is

name: Straw man vs red herring
q: How does a straw man differ from a red herring?
ans:
Straw man: misrepresents the original argument, then attacks the distortion
Red herring: changes the subject to a different topic
Both are most evident in how we respond to others

name: False equivalence
q: What is the false equivalence fallacy?
ans:
Presenting two concepts/arguments as the same when the equivalence is not logical
Format: both x and y are the same (even when they are not!)
e.g. apples and oranges are round fruits so must taste the same

name: Slippery slope vs false dichotomy
q: How does a slippery slope differ from a false dichotomy?
clues: Chain to disaster vs only two options
Food trucks vs dogs in apartment
ans:
Slippery slope: allowing x will lead to a bad/disastrous y
False dichotomy: claims only two possibilities exist
Neither has evidence for its claim

name: Strategies for arguing
q: What questions guide the construction of good arguments (strategies for arguing)?
ans:
Can you build a valid, sound and relevant argument? If not, a strong one?
Are you supporting it with facts?
Are you committing any fallacies?
Are you being generous with the other person's argument?
Are you arguing, or being verbally aggressive?

name: Tools from the three logic lectures
q: What tools does each of the three logic lectures contribute to making arguments?
ans:
Deductive lecture: standard form; validity/proper structure
Inductive lecture: using evidence to strengthen arguments; enhancing generalizability
Fallacies lecture: common errors in reasoning and how to avoid them
Psychology has few absolutes
